citations.note: A whole-species absolute upper adaptability bound (32 °C), broader/later than the already-saved flowering-stage 28 °C damage figure from Bishop et al. 2016. Not contradictory (different stages/metrics); complementary context only. The ECOCROP tutorial (.research-sources/2026-11-06/ecocrop-tutorial.pdf, p.2) defines TOPMN/TOPMX as 'the optimal growing temperature adaptability range (the range of temperatures under which the plant will grow optimally)' and TMIN/TMAX as part of 'the full growing temperature adaptability range (the full range of temperatures under which the plant will grow)... All entries are absolute values.' Neither definition states a daily-maximum or daily-minimum air-temperature basis, a duration, or a growth stage; ECOCROP's underlying climate matching (Hijmans et al.) compares these to long-run mean monthly temperatures, not single-day extremes. TMIN/TMAX are therefore NOT used here as whole-cycle damage limits outright; they are recorded as the closest FAO-tier evidence with this basis gap explicit in missingFields. The builder could not re-find the quote in the saved text, so it is not reproduced.

references.summary: Cool-season annual legume; dry grain differs from green-pod production. Flowers and young pods can be more vulnerable to frost than established vegetative tissue. Heat and moisture stress during flowering and pod set can cause poor set and flower or pod loss. Cereal breaks can reduce some legume pathogen carryover; a different legume is not automatically a non-host. Effective nodulation supports nitrogen fixation; waterlogging and inadequate aeration impair roots and nodules.

citations.quote: Field experiments in Morocco offer compelling evidence. Integrating legumes like lentils, chickpeas, and faba beans into cereal systems reduces nitrogen fertilizer needs by 25% through biological nitrogen fixation—legumes naturally extract nitrogen from the atmosphere, benefiting both the legume crop and the cereal crop planted afterward. This approach not only lowers GHG emissions but also boosts biodiversity, enhances soil health, and increases carbon sequestration, all of which contribute to stronger rural livelihoods.
